What separates elite performers from high performers in any domain?

Anders Ericsson's deliberate practice research: not hours but quality of practice. Deliberate practice characteristics: 1) Outside comfort zone — practice at the edge of current capability. 2) Immediate, accurate feedback. 3) Focused attention — not mindless repetition. 4) Teacher/coach who designs practice. Elite performers in chess, music, sports, medicine all show: 10,000+ hours of deliberate practice (not just experience). Key differentiators beyond practice: Mental representations: experts have richer, more organized mental models of their domain — they see patterns where novices see chaos. Chase/Simon chess studies: experts reconstruct real positions from 5-second exposure with ~90% accuracy, random positions with same as novices. The mental representation IS the expertise. Psychological resilience: elite performers maintain composure under pressure through psychological skills training — visualization, pre-performance routines, attention control. Growth mindset (Dweck): belief that ability develops through effort. Fixed mindset people avoid challenge. Coachability: elite performers remain coachable even at peak — seeking feedback at the highest skill levels. Marginal gains philosophy (Dave Brailsford, British Cycling): 1% improvements across all variables compound. Recovery as part of training: sleep, nutrition, mental rest. Non-negotiable for sustained elite performance.

How do you execute under extreme uncertainty and time pressure?

Situation Assessment under time pressure: use heuristic judgment based on pattern recognition rather than analytical comparison. Recognition-primed decision making (Klein) — experts match situation to stored patterns, retrieve satisfactory response, mentally simulate it, adjust if needed. Satisficing over optimizing: in time-critical situations, first workable option is better than waiting for optimal. Don't let perfect be the enemy of good. Commander's Intent: make the goal explicit and understood so that subordinates can take correct initiative when communications fail. The 'why' must be clear. Simplification under stress: cognitive load rises sharply under time pressure. Pre-simplified decision trees, checklists, drills take decision-making load off working memory. Military: battle drills practiced until automatic. Action bias vs deliberation: research shows people take suboptimal action when deliberation is the right call. Recognize when pause-and-assess is the right action. Two-speed planning: immediate action to establish control, then transition to deliberate planning as situation stabilizes. Debrief every execution: what was intended, what happened, what was the difference, what will change. Under extreme pressure the system defaults to trained behavior — what you train is what you get when it counts.
